```{r}
#| label: tutorials
# Both tracks are built from each tutorial's own front matter. Anything dated
# in the future is a draft: it's listed under "Coming next" without a link.
read_track <- function(files, number_field) {
  items <- lapply(files, \(f) {
    m <- rmarkdown::yaml_front_matter(f)
    m$href <- sub(paste0("^", here::here(), "/"), "", f)
    m$number <- as.numeric(m[[number_field]])
    m
  })
  items[order(vapply(items, \(m) m$number, numeric(1)))]
}
published <- function(items) Filter(\(m) as.Date(m$date) <= Sys.Date(), items)
drafts    <- function(items) Filter(\(m) as.Date(m$date) >  Sys.Date(), items)

capitalise <- function(x) paste0(toupper(substring(x, 1, 1)), substring(x, 2))

tutorial_cards <- function(items, label) {
  if (length(items) == 0) return(invisible())
  cat(sprintf('\n<details class="pub-group">\n<summary>Latest: %s</summary>\n\n', items[[length(items)]]$title))
  cat("::: {.tutorial-cards}\n\n")
  for (m in items) {
    tags <- paste(sprintf("[%s]{.article-tag}", unlist(m$categories)), collapse = " ")
    cat(
      "::: {.pub-card .tutorial-card}\n",
      sprintf("[%s %s]{.pub-year}\n\n", label, m$number),
      sprintf("### [%s](%s) {.pub-title}\n\n", m$title, m$href),
      sprintf("%s\n\n", capitalise(sub("^Tutorial [0-9]+: ", "", m$subtitle))),
      sprintf("%s\n\n", tags),
      ":::\n\n", sep = ""
    )
  }
  cat(":::\n\n</details>\n\n")
}
upcoming <- function(numbers, texts) {
  cat("::: {.series-upcoming}\n")
  for (i in seq_along(numbers)) {
    cat("::: {.upcoming-item}\n",
        sprintf("[%s]{.upcoming-number}\n", numbers[i]),
        sprintf("[%s]{.upcoming-text}\n", texts[i]),
        ":::\n\n", sep = "")
  }
  cat(":::\n")
}

r_track  <- read_track(Sys.glob(here::here("tutorials", "0*", "*.qmd")), "order")
cli_track <- read_track(Sys.glob(here::here("tutorials", "command-line", "*", "index.qmd")), "series-part")
```

There are two tracks, and you can start either one. Each is a series: work through its parts in order, because each builds on the last.

## Bioinformatics on the command line

![](tutorials/images/command-line-series.jpg){.series-banner fig-alt="Illustration of a DNA double helix turning into a network of connected points, with circular genome plots in the background"}

::: {.series-about}
#### <i class="bi bi-info-circle"></i> About this track

**What you'll learn:** working in a Linux terminal, finding and downloading public sequencing data, the file formats of genomics, read quality control and alignment, step by step.

**The data:** real, public whole-genome sequencing of *Mycobacterium tuberculosis* from a study in the Western Cape (European Nucleotide Archive project [PRJEB43283](https://www.ebi.ac.uk/ena/browser/view/PRJEB43283)), and the H37Rv reference genome. Part 2 shows how to find and download it.

**You'll need:** a terminal (Ubuntu or another Linux, macOS, or Windows with WSL) and micromamba to install the tools. Part 1 covers both.
:::

```{r}
#| label: cli-track
#| output: asis
tutorial_cards(published(cli_track), "Part")
```

## Data science

![](tutorials/images/tutorial-series.jpg){.series-banner fig-alt="Illustration of CSV files flowing into an R cube and across to a Python cube"}

::: {.series-about}
#### <i class="bi bi-info-circle"></i> About this track

**What you'll learn:** data analysis and modelling in R and Python: importing and cleaning study data in RStudio, working with the same data in pandas, statistical tests, and later machine learning.

**The dataset:** 500 fictional participants from a simulated bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) study, with participant metadata and cell counts for each study visit. The raw files are deliberately messy, like real study data. No row describes a real person.

[<i class="bi bi-download"></i> bal_metadata.xlsx](tutorials/data/bal_metadata.xlsx){.btn .btn-sm .btn-outline-primary}
[<i class="bi bi-download"></i> bal_cell_counts.xlsx](tutorials/data/bal_cell_counts.xlsx){.btn .btn-sm .btn-outline-primary}
[<i class="bi bi-download"></i> bal_baseline.csv](tutorials/data/bal_baseline.csv){.btn .btn-sm .btn-outline-primary}

**You'll need:** R and RStudio for every tutorial, plus Python from Tutorial 2 onwards.

**Quick guide:** [<i class="bi bi-file-earmark-pdf"></i> Choosing the right statistical test](guides/choosing-a-statistical-test/choosing-a-statistical-test.pdf), a two-page PDF that goes with Tutorial 4.
:::
